summary: RADIUS was running short of room in its 8-bit Attribute Type space, and experience showed a need for grouping attributes and carrying more than 253 octets of data. This document defines changes to RADIUS to solve these problems.

eli5.summary: A form for filling in details ran out of boxes and the boxes were too small. This adds more boxes, groups of boxes, and bigger ones.

subtitle: How RADIUS got more attribute numbers, grouped attributes and values longer than 253 octets without breaking old software.

tldr.problem: RADIUS identifies each attribute with a one-octet Type, and the authors expected that space to be exhausted by 2014 or 2015. Attributes were also stuck at 253 octets of data, and the old grouping method had proved impractical.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses six reserved Type codes (241 to 246) as containers. Each steals the first octet of its Value as an Extended-Type, which gives a new space of type codes, and the long variant adds a flag so one value can be split across several consecutive attributes. New tlv, evs and integer64 data types add nesting, vendor space and 64-bit counters.
tldr.outcome: RADIUS now has room for new attributes, a standard way to group them and a standard way to carry long values. The RFC admits it offers no incentive to adopt it beyond exhaustion of the standard space, and it warns that many proxies mishandle unknown attributes.

today: RFC 6929 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013; the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 2865, RFC 3575 and RFC 6158.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Needed Extending
sections.content:
RADIUS carries its data in attributes, and each attribute has a one-octet Type. The authors expected that Attribute Type space to be exhausted by 2014 or 2015. Other problems had shown up as well: the attribute grouping method in RFC 2868 was impractical, several attributes carried more than the 253 octets the protocol originally envisioned (each handled as a special case in implementations), and some vendors were close to using up their Vendor-Specific Attribute space.

The RFC answers all of this with a set of related changes: an Extended Type format, a Long Extended Type format with fragmentation, a new tlv data type for grouping, a new evs (Extended-Vendor-Specific) data type, a new integer64 data type, and a Vendor-Id that uses all 4 octets.

The authors say the changes are the result of compromises between flexibility, space in the message, compatibility with deployments and difficulty of implementation. They recommend that implementations support the specification and that new specifications use its formats, because otherwise nobody implements it for lack of users and nobody uses it for lack of implementations.
sections.eli5: RADIUS was running out of numbers to label its pieces of information. It also could not hold big pieces or neat groups. This RFC fixes all three problems at once.

sections.title: Extended and Long Extended Attributes
sections.content:
The new formats keep the normal Type and Length octets and "steal" bytes from the Value field. That is why old implementations can still skip or forward them. In the Extended Type format, the first octet of the Value is an Extended-Type. The identifier Type.Extended-Type then decides how the rest of the Value is read. Length runs from 4 to 255, and a text or string value shrinks from 253 to 252 octets. Extended-Type values 1 to 240 are available; 241 to 255 are reserved and must not be used.

The Long Extended Type format adds one more octet after the Extended-Type: a 1-bit M (More) flag and 7 reserved bits. When a value does not fit, the sender sets M, uses a Length of 255 and continues in the next attribute, which must have the same Type and Extended-Type. Fragments must be in order, and the last attribute in a packet must not have M set. Fragments cannot span packets, so the largest value is limited only by the RADIUS packet length limit of 4096 octets, and an implementation must handle one fragmented attribute that fills the whole packet. The receiver reassembles the fragments before interpreting the data, and Length only covers the single fragment.

Fragments may be mixed with attributes of other types, as RFC 2865 never required attributes of one type to be contiguous. Receivers must be able to process such non-contiguous fragments.
sections.eli5: Some labels now have a small sticker inside saying what they really are. If a message is too long for one label, it is cut into pieces on labels in a row, and a flag says whether more pieces follow.

sections.title: TLV, EVS and Integer64 Data Types
sections.content:
The tlv data type lets the Value of an attribute contain sub-attributes, each with a TLV-Type octet, a TLV-Length octet (between 3 and 255) and a value. TLVs can contain other TLVs, and a container TLV must be filled exactly by its contents. A TLV value is limited to 253 or fewer octets. Nesting is technically limited to 126 levels, but more than 4 levels are not recommended. Extended Type attributes may not be nested inside a TLV, and multiple TLVs of the same type are read as an unordered set (a logical "and").

The evs data type is for vendor-specific information. It holds a 4-octet Vendor-Id (the Private Enterprise Code in network byte order), a one-octet EVS-Type that the vendor assigns, and the vendor data. Unlike the Vendor-Specific Attribute in RFC 2865 there is no Vendor-Length field; the length is implied by the attribute Length. It may only appear in Extended Type or Long Extended Type attributes, and the RFC recommends vendors use it only once their ordinary Vendor-Specific Attribute space is fully allocated.

The integer64 data type carries a 64-bit unsigned integer in network byte order, for counters that need to go past 2^32. It is expected mostly in Accounting-Request packets. Finally, the Vendor-Id field of Vendor-Specific Attributes is defined as the full 4 octets rather than 3 plus a zero octet, and implementations are recommended to support that.
sections.eli5: A TLV is a labelled box that can hold smaller labelled boxes, like a toolbox with trays. Vendors get their own special boxes, and there is a bigger number type for counting very high.

sections.title: Dotted Names for Attributes
sections.content:
To talk about the new attributes in specifications, the RFC defines a dotted number notation similar to Object Identifiers. An attribute is written Type.Extended-Type, for example 241.1 or 246.10. A TLV inside it adds another number, such as 241.1.1 or 245.2.3.4 for a TLV nested inside a TLV.

The same notation can be used for Vendor-Specific Attributes as 26.Vendor-Id.Vendor-Type. The text gives 26.307.6 for Livingston's IP-Pool attribute and 26.429.32768 for a USR attribute. The notation is meant for specifications only and imposes nothing on implementations. The RFC also recommends names that are globally unique, such as a vendor-name prefix.
sections.eli5: Each label gets an address like a street number followed by a flat number and a room number, so everyone can point at exactly the same one.

sections.title: Invalid Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC defines an invalid attribute: its Length is acceptable, so the packet is not malformed, but the Value does not match the format its data type requires. An example is an "address" attribute that holds more or fewer than four octets. An invalid attribute must not cause the whole packet to be discarded or treated as a negative acknowledgment. Instead, only that attribute is treated specially.

An invalid attribute should be silently discarded, except when the implementation is a proxy. If it is kept, it must not be handled like a well-formed attribute. Invalidity should not spread upward to an enclosing attribute, but a TLV that requires particular sub-TLVs should itself be treated as invalid if one is missing, wrong or invalid. Attributes with an unknown Type, Extended-Type, TLV-Type or EVS-Type are recommended to be treated as invalid.
sections.eli5: If one item on an order form is filled in wrongly, you throw away that one item and keep reading the rest of the form, instead of tearing up the whole form.

sections.title: Compatibility and Proxies
sections.content:
Some vendors had used the reserved Type codes in their own dictionaries, which RFC 6158 calls antisocial. The RFC recommends removing those definitions, or at least giving servers a per-client flag between "Non-Standard Attributes" and "IETF Attributes" (extended format), with the extended format as default. Clients must not send improperly defined attributes and must read replies as Extended Attributes.

Proxy servers must forward attributes in the new format even if they cannot decode them, and should forward unknown or invalid attributes verbatim. The RFC reports testing through EDUROAM in 2010: of 70 proxies, 17 (24%) filtered unknown or oddly sized attributes, 8 (11%) truncated them, 1 (1%) discarded the request, and 44 (63%) passed them verbatim. It is therefore expected to be difficult to use the format widely until non-conformant proxies are fixed, and proxies that do not support 241 to 246 are recommended to treat them as type "string".

The RFC also updates the data-type guidelines of RFC 6158: unsigned 64-bit integers are now permitted, nested attributes using the extended format may be used, and complex data types should be decomposed into TLVs. For Diameter gateways, the new formats are treated just like traditional RADIUS attributes, so no change is needed.
sections.eli5: Mail carriers in the middle sometimes throw away letters in a shape they do not know. The RFC asks them to pass those letters along untouched, because the person at the end may understand them.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA moved six Attribute Type values from Reserved to Allocated: 241 to 244 as Extended-Type-1 to 4 (short extended space) and 245 and 246 as Long-Extended-Type-1 and 2 (long extended space). Each gives 255 new values of the form TYPE.1 through TYPE.255. In each, value 26 is assigned as Extended-Vendor-Specific, which is for Private Use and not managed by IANA, and values 241 to 255 are reserved.

Allocating from the reserved entries needs Standards Action, and all other allocations in the extended space need IETF Review. The guidelines say that an attribute with 252 octets or less of data may use the short extended space, an attribute that always has less than 253 octets must not use the long space, and an attribute with 253 or more octets must use the long space. Specifications that would allocate 20% or more of the remaining standard space should use the extended space, and attributes of data type TLV should be allocated from the extended space.
sections.eli5: The number registry keeper set aside six special boxes. Each one opens up a whole new shelf of numbered slots, and the keeper decides who gets which slot.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines new formats for data carried in RADIUS and otherwise makes no change to the protocol's security. It notes that RADIUS depends on MD5, which has known issues described in RFC 6151, and that it is not known whether those issues apply to RADIUS. It also incorporates the security considerations of RFC 6158 by reference.

New code can introduce new vulnerabilities, and because a RADIUS server performs network authentication it is an inviting target. The RFC recommends keeping access to RADIUS servers to a minimum. Elsewhere it warns that very deep TLV nesting may indicate implementation errors or deliberate attacks.
sections.eli5: New parts can have new cracks, and the guard desk is a tempting target, so only a few people should be allowed near it.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Identical to the RFC 2865 Type field; 245 or 246 for long extended attributes.

fields.name: Extended-Type
fields.desc: Type space within the Type; 241 to 255 are reserved.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: More flag: set when the value continues in the next attribute (Length must be 255).

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero when sending; ignored on reception.

items.desc: Long Extended Type format, supports fragmentation.
